questions.stem: What does Porter define as the primary goal of Operational Effectiveness (OE)?

options.A: Performing similar activities better than rivals.
options.B: Making necessary trade-offs.
options.C: Expanding market share in high-growth segments.
options.D: Achieving a unique market position.

questions.explanation: OE is defined as performing similar activities better—improving quality, efficiency, and speed. It is distinct from Strategy, which is about performing different activities.

questions.stem: Tesla's initial Roadster/Model S launch strategy aligns best with which of Porter's competitive forces relative to the auto industry?

options.A: Threat of New Entrants (EVs being non-traditional for the auto industry).
options.B: Threat of Substitutes (EVs replace ICE cars).
options.C: Bargaining Power of Buyers (Customers demanding EVs).
options.D: Rivalry Among Existing Competitors (Direct head-to-head competition).

questions.explanation: By creating a superior, high-performance electric car, Tesla offered a powerful substitute for traditional gasoline luxury cars, changing the basis of competition.

questions.stem: The 'production hell' faced during the Model 3 ramp-up is a clear failure of:

options.A: Strategic Positioning.
options.B: Vertical Integration as a Trade-off.
options.C: Operational Effectiveness (OE).
options.D: Customer segmentation.

questions.explanation: The chaos, rework, and lack of efficiency were failures of Operational Effectiveness—the system was not performing the manufacturing activity well.

questions.stem: Why did Tesla's Direct Sales Model create a crucial strategic advantage (a competitive barrier) over legacy automakers?

options.A: It was cheaper than hiring commissioned sales agents.
options.B: It eliminated all capital costs for distribution.
options.C: It forced all legacy rivals to immediately adopt the model.
options.D: It bypassed the dealer network whose profit model ($\\sim 60\\%$ from service/parts) was fundamentally misaligned with low-maintenance EVs.

questions.explanation: The dealer profit model created a structural conflict for incumbents, making Tesla's direct sales a powerful structural advantage (Trade-off) that rivals could not easily copy without facing massive internal conflict.

questions.stem: Tesla's remarkably high R&D spending (over $\\mathbf{11\\%}$ of revenue) is BEST justified by its strategy as a requirement for:

options.A: Sustaining Vertical Integration and technology control (software, battery IP).
options.B: Reducing labor costs on the factory floor.
options.C: Financing Musk's other ventures (SpaceX, X).
options.D: Achieving market share targets for the Model 3.

questions.explanation: To own and control the battery, AI, and software systems (Vertical Integration), Tesla must maintain this high R&D cost. It is a mandatory cost to sustain its unique strategic Activity System.

questions.stem: The concept of Fit is critical for competitive sustainability because:

options.A: It guarantees the company will always earn a profit.
options.B: It makes the entire Activity System harder to imitate than any single component.
options.C: It forces the company to focus purely on Operational Effectiveness.
options.D: It prevents the CEO from taking any external risks.

questions.explanation: Porter states that when activities are interdependent (Fit), a rival must copy the entire complex system to gain any benefit, making imitation mathematically difficult.

questions.stem: The acquisition of SolarCity created severe Governance risks. Strategically, this acquisition risked violating the principle of:

options.A: The Bargaining Power of Suppliers.
options.B: Operational Effectiveness (OE).
options.C: Trade-offs, by diverting resources and focus from the core Model 3 production crisis.
options.D: Strategic Position, by moving too far from the luxury segment.

questions.explanation: The SolarCity deal forced a clear choice of resource allocation: focus on the existential Model 3 ramp-up or fund the non-core energy business, violating the necessary resource trade-offs.

questions.stem: Why is Musk's 'ultra hardcore' leadership style considered a Trade-off for Tesla?

options.A: It makes the company attractive to all institutional investors.
options.B: It is the only style compatible with selling EVs.
options.C: It guarantees high employee retention and loyalty.
options.D: It substitutes for a robust, standardized Operational Effectiveness system, relying on individual superhuman effort.

questions.explanation: Musk's style is a Trade-off that trades stable, repeatable processes (good OE) for chaotic, high-intensity innovation and push—an unsustainable, but sometimes necessary, lever.

questions.stem: In the simulation, arguing to HIRE AN EXTERNAL CEO is primarily a vote for which strategic component?

options.A: Enhanced Operational Effectiveness and improved Governance.
options.B: The abandonment of the Vertical Integration model.
options.C: New, radical R&D investment.
options.D: Increased market share in the luxury segment.

questions.explanation: An external CEO's value proposition is always professionalizing systems to improve compliance (Governance) and efficiency (OE).

questions.stem: The controversy over working conditions and safety at the Fremont factory (leading to low ESG scores) fundamentally threatens Tesla's core Activity System because:

options.A: It proves that Tesla's battery technology is unsafe.
options.B: It damages the company's brand, raising the cost of capital and alienating institutional investors who prioritize sustainability.
options.C: It means the Model Y is no longer competitive on price.
options.D: It forces the company to outsource all R&D activities.

questions.explanation: Poor ESG scores directly increase the cost of capital and threaten long-term stability by limiting access to institutional investment pools (a failure of the Activity System's Fit with finance).

questions.stem: Porter argues that the sustainability of a strategy relies on Second- and Third-Order Fit. Which of the following best represents a Second-Order Fit activity at Tesla?

options.A: Offering Model S vehicles in red, black, and white.
options.B: Installing robots on the assembly line (Operational Effectiveness).
options.C: Using Direct Sales to control pricing, which reinforces the Over-the-Air Software Updates to build a strong customer relationship.
options.D: Borrowing money from a bank (General Activity).

questions.explanation: The two activities reinforce each other: Direct contact facilitates rapid software deployment, and excellent software validates the direct customer relationship.

questions.stem: The debate over Musk's $\\mathbf{25\\%}$ voting control demand directly relates to the teaching objective concerning:

options.A: The shift in luxury sedan sales market share (Chart 4).
options.B: The necessity of reducing fixed costs.
options.C: Measuring Operational Effectiveness (OE).
options.D: Reflecting on Governance and Growth for founder-led companies.

questions.explanation: This is a core governance issue at a critical growth juncture, directly testing the balance of founder control vs. corporate accountability.

questions.stem: The fact that in $\\mathbf{2017}$, Tesla required 11% of revenue for $\\mathbf{R\\&D}$ while rivals required $\\mathbf{3\\%}$ to $\\mathbf{7\\%}$ suggests that the primary basis of competition in the auto industry has shifted from:

options.A: Operational Effectiveness (low-cost, efficient assembly) to Vertical Integration (owning the tech stack).
options.B: Product quality to marketing expenditure.
options.C: Access-based positioning to needs-based positioning.
options.D: Maximizing production efficiency to maximizing retail sales.

questions.explanation: High R&D is necessary to own the core technology (battery, AI), proving that the battle has moved beyond merely efficient assembly (OE).

questions.stem: If the Board chose the COMPROMISE option (Musk to Executive Chairman), the primary risk, according to Porter, is that the company would violate the core principle of:

options.A: The pursuit of perfect Operational Effectiveness.
options.B: Making clear Trade-offs (risking strategic incoherence).
options.C: Ignoring competitor actions (Benchmarking).
options.D: Eliminating all fixed costs.

questions.explanation: A compromise is an attempt to avoid a clear choice, risking the 'stuck in the middle' syndrome and leading to management indecision and confusion.

questions.stem: The leadership style that is perfect for a scrappy startup seeking Strategic Position (like early Tesla) but is ill-suited for a massive, mature public company is called the Leadership Lifecycle problem. This primarily highlights the need for the right leader to manage the evolving demands of:

options.A: The need to sell the company to a larger rival.
options.B: The company's external lobbying efforts.
options.C: The transition from Strategy-as-Founding Vision to Strategy-as-Sustainable System.
options.D: The market's increasing acceptance of EVs.

questions.explanation: The chaotic, visionary founder is necessary to establish the unique position, but the systematic, disciplined manager is needed to sustain the complex Activity System.

questions.stem: Tesla's low ESG Governance scores directly impact its Strategic Sustainability by:

options.A: Forcing the company to abandon the Supercharger Network.
options.B: Increasing the Bargaining Power of Suppliers.
options.C: Proving that the Model 3 assembly line is less automated than competitors' lines.
options.D: Increasing the Cost of Capital and alienating the large institutional investors needed for future growth, thereby weakening the Activity System's Fit with the financial market.

questions.explanation: Low ESG scores damage the ESG profile, which increases the cost of capital and alienates institutional investors, directly threatening Sustainability.

questions.stem: The fundamental tension of the Leadership Lifecycle is the transition from the founder's visionary style to a professional management team. This transition is difficult because the qualities that create an Outlier Outcome (e.g., Manic Focus, Risk-Taking) are often:

options.A: Structurally incompatible with the Discipline, Accountability, and Institutional Fit required for long-term Governance.
options.B: Directly linked to violating the Trade-off between Direct Sales and Vertical Integration.
options.C: Only necessary during periods of low R&D spending intensity.
options.D: Essential for generating high, repeatable EBITDA margins in a mature market.

questions.explanation: The extreme qualities needed to disrupt are structurally incompatible with the Discipline and Accountability required for institutional stability and OE.

questions.stem: The SEC charges and subsequent penalties imposed on Musk in 2018 (Case, p. 11) function as a critical Governance check which:

options.A: Primarily affected the Operational Effectiveness of the Gigafactory automation system.
options.B: Externally enforced a structural boundary on the founder's behavior, protecting the financial stability and Fit of the company for broader shareholders.
options.C: Required Tesla to abandon its Vertical Integration strategy in battery production.
options.D: Proved that Musk’s focus was entirely on SpaceX.

questions.explanation: The SEC action was an external enforcement of Governance to protect the financial stability required for the firm's strategic Fit.

questions.stem: The SolarCity Acquisition (Case, p. 10), despite being financially disastrous and rife with conflicts of interest, had a singular strategic Defense within the context of the Master Plan, which was:

options.A: To eliminate the Bargaining Power of Buyers.
options.B: To achieve immediate economies of scale in the mass-market EV segment.
options.C: To enforce the Third-Order Fit of the Activity System by integrating the car, battery, and energy generation into one seamless platform.
options.D: To comply with the ESG requirements of the S&P 500 Index.

questions.explanation: The SolarCity acquisition was strategically defended as necessary to complete the Activity System by integrating the car/battery with energy generation (Third-Order Fit).

questions.stem: The Cybertruck and Optimus AI initiatives pose a high Execution Risk but are strategically necessary for Musk's retention in the CEO role because:

options.A: They fully automate the Fremont Factory, eliminating OE failures.
options.B: They minimize R&D Intensity below that of VW.
options.C: They are essential to maintaining the high Gross Margin of the legacy Model S.
options.D: They continuously prove that the company is still in the "Outlier Startup Phase" of the Leadership Lifecycle, justifying the founder's Risk-Taking Trade-off.

questions.explanation: Continuously pushing high-risk visions (Cybertruck, AI) is the primary way a founder justifies their retention, arguing the company is still in the revolutionary Vision phase.

questions.stem: If the Board chooses the Compromise option (Musk as Executive Chairman, operational CEO), the most significant strategic risk, based on organizational sociology and Porter's concept of Fit, is:

options.A: The structural division of authority (vision vs. operations) will lead to strategic Dissonance and Incoherence (a flaw in Fit).
options.B: The SEC will impose higher fines for inadequate Governance.
options.C: The Threat of New Entrants will dramatically increase.
options.D: The new CEO will immediately reverse the Direct Sales Trade-off.

questions.explanation: Dividing Vision (Chairman) from Execution (CEO) risks creating systemic Dissonance and Incoherence (a flaw in Fit), undermining organizational priorities.

questions.stem: Which scenario best demonstrates Second-Order Fit (where two distinct activities reinforce each other to create a unique value)?

options.A: The elimination of Fixed Costs in distribution.
options.B: High R&D Investment reinforces the development of Superior Battery Life, which increases the car's desirability to customers.
options.C: The use of robots to weld the chassis faster than manual laborers.
options.D: A company making the Trade-off to forgo hot meals on an airline.

questions.explanation: High R&D enables Superior Battery Life, which in turn reinforces the core Differentiation Position.

questions.stem: Tesla’s continued high R&D intensity is vital for its Strategic Position, but the persistent Governance issues (SEC, ESG) threaten its Sustainability. This paradox suggests that the firm must make a Trade-off between:

options.A: The Threat of Substitutes and Rivalry Among Existing Competitors.
options.B: Operational Effectiveness and Strategy as mutually exclusive goals.
options.C: Radical Innovation (Strategy) and the Financial and Social Stability (Governance) needed to realize that innovation.
options.D: The Leadership Lifecycle problem and external oversight.

questions.explanation: The paradox is the strategic Trade-off between the short-term necessity of Radical Innovation and the long-term imperative of Financial and Social Stability.

questions.stem: The demand for increased voting control directly relates to the teaching objective concerning Governance and Growth because it tests the balance between:

options.A: The low R&D spending of rivals versus Tesla’s high expenditure.
options.B: The Threat of Substitutes versus the Bargaining Power of Buyers.
options.C: Maximizing Operational Effectiveness (OE) versus increasing Vertical Integration.
options.D: The Vision and Risk-Taking of an Outlier Leader versus the Checks and Balances needed for Sustainable Corporate Governance.

questions.explanation: The 25% Control demand tests the balance between the Vision of an Outlier Leader and the necessary Governance Checks and Balances required for a mature public company.

questions.stem: Tesla's successful entry strategy (high-end Roadster → mass-market Model 3) fundamentally challenged the auto industry by forcing incumbents to confront which crucial strategic dilemma, according to Porter?

options.A: The trade-off between prioritizing Operational Effectiveness (OE) (efficient ICE assembly) and making radical strategic choices necessary to compete on a new basis (technology stack).
options.B: The erosion of buyer power caused by the rise of electric vehicle substitutes.
options.C: The necessity of increasing EBITDA growth to match Tesla's valuation.
options.D: Whether to maximize economies of scale or economies of scope.

questions.lo: The Core Conflict of Strategic Position

questions.stem: The financial conflict associated with the SolarCity Acquisition (high cost, low immediate return) risked violating which core Porterian principle in the most severe way during the Model 3 ramp-up?

options.A: The difficulty of achieving First-Order Fit in supply chain logistics.
options.B: The necessity of making a clear Trade-off of managerial attention and capital, risking resources being diverted from the core existential mission (Model 3).
options.C: The threat of substitutes in the energy market.
options.D: The inability to benchmark core R&D effectively.

questions.stem: Which scenario best demonstrates Second-Order Fit within Tesla's Activity System?

options.A: Musk's personal brand attracting both engineering talent and retail investors.
options.B: The Cybertruck's steel exoskeleton making it cheaper to manufacture than the Model Y.
options.C: The use of Over-the-Air Software Updates to improve performance, which simultaneously reinforces the Direct Sales Model by centralizing the customer relationship and capturing data.
options.D: Achieving profitability in Q3 2018 after maximizing production volume.

questions.stem: The traditional franchised dealer network initially represented an "insurmountable barrier" for new auto entrants. Tesla negated this barrier not by matching it, but by:

options.A: Outspending incumbents on national television advertising.
options.B: Achieving superior Operational Effectiveness in gasoline engine production.
options.C: Creating an entirely new Variety-Based Positioning that targeted only non-luxury buyers.
options.D: Employing a superior Direct Sales Trade-off that was structurally incompatible with the incumbent Activity System (dealer service profits).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most precise Porterian definition of the long-term Strategic Position Tesla has sought since Master Plan Part I?

options.A: A focus strategy based on a unique Activity System that treats the vehicle as a vertically integrated Software and Energy Platform (Variety and Needs-Based).
options.B: Access-based positioning by serving rural markets through cheap infrastructure.
options.C: Achieving Operational Effectiveness across all dimensions of the value chain.
options.D: Cost leadership through maximizing production automation.

questions.stem: In the final simulation, the primary strategic risk of choosing the Compromise option (Musk as Chairman, External CEO) is the introduction of Dissonance that threatens Fit, similar to the Yahoo case. This happens because:

options.A: The external CEO will inevitably increase R&D spending too quickly.
options.B: The two leaders’ objectives will clash: one pushing radical, high-risk Strategy, and the other demanding stable, risk-averse Operational Discipline.
options.C: The market will view the external CEO as a mere figurehead, ignoring their efforts entirely.
options.D: It triples the company’s CAPEX requirements for the Gigafactory.

questions.stem: Musk's intense, demanding leadership (the "super hardcore" culture) is best analyzed as a leadership style that:

options.A: Is primarily designed to reduce the Bargaining Power of Suppliers.
options.B: Is entirely irrelevant to the competitive advantage, which relies solely on technology.
options.C: Substitutes for robust, institutionalized Operational Effectiveness by relying on individual human effort and pressure to push the radical, unproven Vertical Integration System forward.
options.D: Violates the core tenet of Vertical Integration but satisfies Governance.

questions.stem: Tesla’s commitment to high R&D Intensity (Exhibit A) is a clear example of Second-Order Fit because it:

options.A: Reduces the Threat of New Entrants by increasing the cost of Vertical Integration.
options.B: Is entirely driven by compliance with US Federal Emissions Standards.
options.C: Aligns with the low-cost strategy required to compete with Toyota.
options.D: Mutually reinforces the Direct Sales Model by consistently providing advanced software features (OTA Updates) that justify bypassing the dealer experience.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be an example of First-Order Fit (simple consistency) in Tesla's strategy?

options.A: All activities, from R&D to manufacturing, being aligned with the overall goal of EV Technology Leadership.
options.B: The SolarCity acquisition and Tesla Energy creating a combined power wall product.
options.C: The company hiring a new CEO known for Operational Discipline.
options.D: The founder's political opinions aligning with the company mission.

questions.stem: The constant tension between Vision (Strategy) and Accountability (Governance) highlights the high organizational price of achieving a dramatic Strategic Position, as the successful implementation of radical strategy often requires:

options.A: The total elimination of all Vertical Integration.
options.B: A temporary tolerance for OE Failures and Governance Abreactions that would destroy a conventionally managed firm.
options.C: A shift from Needs-Based Positioning to Access-Based Positioning.
options.D: The complete compliance with all ESG rating requirements from day one.

questions.stem: Musk's dual commitments to non-Tesla ventures (SpaceX, X/Twitter) create significant strategic risk for Tesla because they:

options.A: Automatically trigger a reduction in the Threat of New Entrants.
options.B: Directly violate the Vertical Integration Trade-off.
options.C: Divert scarce Capital and Management Attention from the core Activity System, thereby imposing an external Cost that damages the firm's internal Fit and Sustainability.
options.D: Force the entire auto industry to adopt AI Robotics.

questions.lo: Strategic Risk from Non-Core Ventures (Attention/Resource Cost)

questions.stem: Based on the case evidence (Zip2, X.com, Tesla), which leadership characteristic is consistently presented as both the source of Musk’s Outlier Outcomes and his greatest Governance Risk?

options.A: The ability to eliminate all Trade-offs.
options.B: A commitment to Variety-Based Positioning.
options.C: Extreme deference to Operational Effectiveness metrics.
options.D: Maniacal Focus and Dominance, leading to both miraculous execution and organizational burnout/conflict.

questions.stem: Musk's demand for employees to be "super hardcore" (Case, p. 7) is a management practice that directly attempts to compensate for a deficit in which area of the firm's operations?

options.A: The lack of Institutionalized Operational Effectiveness (standardized, repeatable, high-quality processes).
options.B: The limited success of the initial Roadster platform.
options.C: The inability to negotiate low prices with Tier 1 Suppliers.
options.D: The difficulty of making a clear Strategic Position choice.

questions.lo: The "Ultra Hardcore" Style and OE (Execution vs. System)

questions.stem: The Q2 2018 Net Loss of 717.5} million (Exhibit 11a), despite rising revenue, is the ultimate financial measure of the failure of:

options.A: The Bargaining Power of Buyers.
options.B: The Third-Order Fit of the company's Activity System to eliminate redundancy in production and quality control.
options.C: The inability to increase the price of the Model 3 above 35,000}.
options.D: The Trade-off associated with the SolarCity Acquisition.

questions.explanation: The massive Net Loss demonstrates the fundamental failure of Operational Effectiveness in production—the high costs of rework and chaos crippled profitability.

questions.stem: If legacy automakers can achieve similar R&D levels by 2022, the most enduring non-imitable strategic difference created by Tesla's initial Trade-offs remains:

options.A: The founder's ownership stake (13%), which is irrelevant to firm operations.
options.B: Its ability to produce the Model 3 at a lower cost than GM.
options.C: The fully integrated nature of its Activity System, particularly the relationship between Proprietary Software and the Direct Customer Relationship.
options.D: Its use of the Supercharger Network, which is easily copied by utilities.

questions.stem: Exhibit 11a shows the Model S outselling major luxury incumbents (BMW 7-Series, Audi A8) by 2017. This achievement, despite Tesla's initial financial losses and quality issues (poor OE), suggests that:

options.A: Competitors successfully imitated Tesla's Direct Sales Model immediately.
options.B: Tesla's gross profit margin remained higher than that of luxury incumbents.
options.C: Tesla had already achieved price parity with ICE vehicles.
options.D: The superior value proposition of Tesla's Strategic Position (technology/product stack) commanded sufficient Buyer Willingness to Pay to offset the functional failures in its Operational Effectiveness.

questions.lo: The Model 3 vs. Luxury Rivals (Market Data)

questions.stem: Choosing to RETAIN MUSK as CEO in the simulation (Option A) is fundamentally based on accepting the high cost of the Founder's Paradox because it prioritizes the teaching objective of:

options.A: Analyzing how an individual leader can make a difference revolutionizing a whole industry, viewing the chaos as a necessary byproduct of Risk-taking (Case, p. 2).
options.B: Reflecting on the need for strong Corporate Governance principles (ESG Index).
options.C: Proving that the company has completed the Leadership Lifecycle transition.
options.D: Evaluating the optimal management needed for predictable quarterly earnings (OE).

questions.lo: The Final Dilemma - Leadership vs. System (Synthesis)

questions.stem: The "Valley of Death" in the automotive industry refers to:

options.A: The decline of internal combustion engine sales.
options.B: The period of negative cash flow between capital investment and volume production.
options.C: The failure rate of Tier 2 suppliers during a recession.
options.D: The gap between announcing a model and delivering it to customers.

questions.stem: According to Porter’s Five Forces, which factor historically protected GM and Ford from new entrants?

options.A: Rapid technological innovation cycles.
options.B: Low capital intensity of manufacturing.
options.C: High barriers to entry due to dealer networks and capital costs.
options.D: Weak bargaining power of suppliers.

questions.stem: Step 2 of Musk’s "Secret Master Plan" was specifically to:

options.A: Acquire a solar energy company immediately.
options.B: Integrate AI into manufacturing.
options.C: Build a high-volume car to fund a low-volume car.
options.D: Use money from the sports car to build an affordable car.

questions.stem: Tesla’s acquisition of SolarCity in 2016 is best described strategically as:

options.A: Ecosystem integration aligning with Step 4 of the Master Plan.
options.B: Unrelated diversification to hedge against auto cyclicality.
options.C: Horizontal integration to capture competitor market share.
options.D: Vertical integration to secure battery supply.

questions.stem: In 2017, Tesla’s Gross Margin was approximately 18.9%, while Ford’s was ~10.6%. This indicates:

options.A: Tesla had lower SG&A costs than Ford.
options.B: Tesla had better unit economics but lacked sufficient scale to cover fixed costs.
options.C: Ford was pricing its vehicles aggressively to gain market share.
options.D: Tesla’s "Production Hell" had no impact on financial metrics.

questions.stem: The "Alien Dreadnought" concept failed primarily because:

options.A: Suppliers refused to integrate with the automated system.
options.B: Robots were too expensive to purchase.
options.C: It underestimated the value of human flexibility in undefined processes.
options.D: The factory lacked sufficient electricity supply.

questions.stem: Which structural barrier did Tesla bypass by selling directly to consumers?

options.A: Import tariffs on raw materials.
options.B: EPA emissions regulations.
options.C: NHTSA safety standards.
options.D: Franchise laws protecting third-party dealerships.

questions.stem: The primary strategic risk of Tesla’s 2018 "Production Hell" was:

options.A: Insolvency due to cash burn exceeding capital reserves.
options.B: Loss of intellectual property to Chinese competitors.
options.C: Regulatory crackdown on Autopilot features.
options.D: Brand dilution due to high volume.

questions.stem: Tesla’s decision to build the Gigafactory was a response to:

options.A: A desire to move manufacturing out of California.
options.B: Global supply constraints on lithium-ion batteries.
options.C: Tax incentives offered by the state of Texas exclusively.
options.D: The need to manufacture tires in-house.

questions.stem: In the context of Disruption Theory, Tesla entered the market at the:

options.A: Commercial sector, competing on fleet costs.
options.B: Low end, disrupting via price.
options.C: High end, competing on performance and design.
options.D: Middle market, competing on reliability.

questions.stem: The "Flufferbot" anecdote illustrates a failure in:

options.A: Marketing Communication.
options.B: Supply Chain Logistics.
options.C: Product Design.
options.D: Process Engineering and Automation Strategy.

questions.stem: Tesla’s P/E ratio being significantly higher than GM’s implies investors view it as:

options.A: A high-growth technology platform.
options.B: A cyclical industrial manufacturer.
options.C: A mature value stock with stable dividends.
options.D: A distressed asset with liquidation value.

questions.stem: Which force was NOT a significant barrier to entry for Tesla in 2004?

options.A: Access to capital.
options.B: Access to software talent.
options.C: Access to distribution networks.
options.D: Economies of scale in manufacturing.

questions.stem: The "Tent" (GA4) represented a shift from:

options.A: Fixed costs to variable revenues.
options.B: Lean manufacturing to Mass production.
options.C: Automated rigidity to manual agility.
options.D: In-house production to outsourcing.

questions.stem: Musk’s strategy to "burn the boats" (commit fully) is best exemplified by:

options.A: Diversifying into SpaceX and Boring Company.
options.B: Selling stock to buy Twitter.
options.C: Hiring a traditional automotive CEO.
options.D: Sleeping on the factory floor.

questions.stem: The "Flufferbot" was designed to perform which task?

options.A: Place fiberglass sound-deadening mats on battery packs.
options.B: Polish the exterior paint.
options.C: Connect the high-voltage wiring harness.
options.D: Install seats into the chassis.

questions.stem: Tesla’s "GA4" assembly line was unique because it was:

options.A: Fully automated with no human workers.
options.B: Located in a temporary sprung structure (tent).
options.C: Built underground to save space.
options.D: Outsourced to a third-party manufacturer.

questions.stem: Why did Tesla bring seat manufacturing in-house for the Model X?

options.A: To increase the weight of the vehicle.
options.B: To lower costs by using cheaper materials.
options.C: Because external suppliers failed to deliver the complex "monopost" design.
options.D: To comply with union regulations.

questions.stem: Musk admitted that "excessive automation" was a mistake because:

options.A: The electricity costs were too high.
options.B: The robots were hacking the software.
options.C: Robots were too slow compared to humans.
options.D: Humans are better at dealing with unexpected variances and anomalies.

questions.stem: A traditional automotive OEM typically outsources what percentage of the vehicle value?
The "Alien Dreadnought" concept aimed to maximize:

options.A: Production quality.
options.B: Volumetric velocity (speed of the line).
options.C: Worker safety.
options.D: Aesthetic appeal of the factory.

questions.stem: In 2018, Tesla’s primary operational bottleneck was in:

options.A: Solar roof tile installation.
options.B: Demand generation (sales).
options.C: General Assembly of the Model 3.
options.D: Software development.

questions.stem: The "Monopost" seat design in the Model X was difficult because:

options.A: It used leather that was illegal in California.
options.B: It was too light for safety regulations.
options.C: It blocked the driver's rear view.
options.D: It required a single pedestal rather than rails, demanding tight tolerances.

questions.stem: Which manufacturing metric was critical for Tesla to achieve profitability in Q3 2018?

options.A: 5,000 cars/week.
options.B: 10,000 cars/week.
options.C: 1,000 cars/week.
options.D: 2,500 cars/week.

questions.stem: Vertical integration of battery production (Gigafactory) allows Tesla to:

options.A: Increase the cost per kWh.
options.B: Control the cell chemistry and reduce supply chain dependency.
options.C: Eliminate the need for lithium.
options.D: Outsource the BMS (Battery Management System).

questions.stem: Unlike ICE vehicles, an electric vehicle powertrain typically has:

options.A: More moving parts (2,000+).
options.B: A complex multi-gear transmission.
options.C: Fewer moving parts (~20) and a single-speed transmission.
options.D: A catalytic converter.

questions.stem: The "Sprung structure" (Tent) took approximately how long to build?

options.A: 6 months.
options.B: 1 year.
options.C: 2 years.
options.D: 3 weeks.

questions.stem: Tesla’s approach to "beta testing" the Model 3 production line was:

options.A: Skipped entirely to save time ("building the airplane while flying").
options.B: Outsourced to Magna Steyr.
options.C: Virtual simulation only.
options.D: Standard 6-month pilot run.

questions.stem: Which component did Tesla notoriously struggle to weld during the Model 3 ramp?

options.A: The aluminum chassis.
options.B: The steel body-in-white.
options.C: The plastic bumper.
